extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and practitioners subject to USPTO disciplinary/reciprocal-discipline proceedings; counsel handling OED matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used by the USPTO Director (OED) to determine whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication and the limits on a respondent's defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-discipline presumption under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the specified Selling elements exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a presumption in favor of imposing the same discipline the state imposed; respondent must overcome this by clear and convincing evidence raising a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the enumerated defenses. The Director considers any timely filed response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (i): Deprivation of due process (notice/opportunity to be heard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires reasonable notice of the charges and an opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner (e.g., ability to present evidence, testify, cross-examine, and argue). Mere disagreement with the state's interpretation of rules does not establish a due-process deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (ii): Infirmity of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult showing: the respondent must present clear and convincing evidence of an infirmity so substantial that the USPTO cannot accept the state's factual conclusion. Disagreements about credibility or legal conclusions typically do not meet this standard; deference is given to trier-of-fact credibility findings. Summary judgment is appropriate when no factual disputes remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (iii): Grave injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that imposing identical discipline would cause a grave injustice. The standard is narrow and rarely met; mere disagreement with penalty severity is insufficient unless it rises to clear-and-convincing proof of grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling element (iv): No public discipline by state
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the state did not impose public discipline (or the discipline was mischaracterized), that is a discrete defense; respondent must raise a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence to avoid identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (respondent)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal discipline cases, it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal/USPTO practice treats this standard as narrow; courts and the Director will require clear-and-convincing proof and are not sitting as a court of review to discover legal error in the state's proceedings (citations: In re Kramer; In re Friedman; Zdravkovich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Due-process particulars in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific due-process protections include reasonable notice of charges, ability to be represented by counsel, ability to present evidence, testify, cross-examine witnesses, make objections, and present argument. Attendance and active participation in hearings weigh strongly against a due-process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of summary judgment in disciplinary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are no remaining factual questions in an attorney-discipline proceeding, summary judgment is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grant of summary judgment is proper when uncontested, dispositive facts exist (e.g., admissions or documentary proof). The absence of factual disputes can mean no further adjudicatory hearing is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to trier-of-fact credibility findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations by the trier-of-fact regarding the credibility of witnesses generally receive deference; a disagreement about credibility does not establish an infirmity of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent cannot overturn state findings simply by disputing witness credibility; must show clear-and-convincing evidence of infirmity in proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Florida Rule 4-4.2 — Communication with person represented by counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: In representing a client, a lawyer must not communicate about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer knows to be represented by another lawyer in the matter, unless the lawyer has the consent of the other lawyer. Notwithstanding the foregoing, a lawyer may, without such prior consent, communicate with another's client to meet the requirements of any court rule, statute or contract requiring notice or service of process directly on a person, in which event the communication is strictly restricted to that required and a copy must be provided to the person's lawyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allowable exception is narrow and strictly limited to communications required for notice/service; forwarding a response to a grievance does not authorize broader settlement negotiation or discussion of unrelated litigation topics. Admission that the recipient is represented, plus communications about the underlying litigation or disparaging opposing counsel, establishes a Rule 4-4.2 violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Florida Rule 4-8.4(d) — Conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer shall not engage in conduct in connection with the practice of law that is prejudicial to the administration of justice, including to knowingly, or through callous indifference, disparage, humiliate, or discriminate against litigants, jurors, witnesses, court personnel, or other lawyers on any basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disparaging or insulting statements about opposing counsel (e.g., calling counsel 'scum') can violate Rule 4-8.4(d). The rule contains no truth-based exception; truthful statements that disparage another lawyer do not immunize misconduct from discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro se representation does not negate 'representing a client' status
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer representing himself pro se is still 'representing a client' for purposes of rules prohibiting communications with persons known to be represented by counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pro se status does not permit direct contact with opposing represented parties; courts and ethics opinions find a pro se attorney still holds an advantage and is subject to the same restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation privilege does not bar disciplinary measures for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made in connection with a pending legal matter are not necessarily privileged from disciplinary action; disciplinary measures remain available for misconduct occurring in judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments invoking litigation immunity to avoid bar discipline are typically insufficient; courts have held disciplinary remedies (and contempt) remain available despite claims of privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible USPTO remedial and administrative actions after discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders can: suspend the respondent from practice before the USPTO for a specified period; require petition for reinstatement under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60; require compliance with duties under § 11.58; dissociate respondent's name from Customer Numbers and USPTO electronic accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order may also direct OED to publish notices and notify state agencies and courts; the Order becomes subject to review (see below) and triggers administrative compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and interagency notice obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.59 and Official Gazette)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall publish a Notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the sample text and give notice of the public discipline and reasons to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the states where respondent is admitted and to courts where respondent is known to be admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions are made available via the OED FOIA Reading Room; publication text typically includes identity, registration number, basis for discipline, and citation to statutory/regulatory authority (35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to judicial review and filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of the final decision by the USPTO Director may be had by a Petition filed with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local civil rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) govern filing; timely filing is jurisdictionally important to seek review.
